claim: Collagens are a primary component of the extracellular matrix.
source: Collagens are a primary component of the extracellular matrix and are functional ligands for the inhibitory immune receptor leukocyte-associated immunoglobulin-like receptor (LAIR)-1.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the composition of the extracellular matrix.

claim: Collagens are functional ligands for LAIR-1.
source: Collagens are a primary component of the extracellular matrix and are functional ligands for the inhibitory immune receptor leukocyte-associated immunoglobulin-like receptor (LAIR)-1.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript (Lebbink et al., 2006; Rygiel et al., 2011).

claim: LAIR-2 is a secreted protein that can act as a decoy receptor by binding collagen with higher affinity than LAIR-1.
source: LAIR-2 is a secreted protein that can act as a decoy receptor by binding collagen with higher affinity than LAIR-1.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript (Lebbink et al., 2008; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2011).

claim: Collagens promote immune evasion by interacting with LAIR-1 expressed on immune cells.
source: We propose that collagens promote immune evasion by interacting with LAIR-1 expressed on immune cells, and that LAIR-2 releases LAIR-1-mediated immune suppression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their understanding of the system.

claim: LAIR-2 releases LAIR-1-mediated immune suppression.
source: We propose that collagens promote immune evasion by interacting with LAIR-1 expressed on immune cells, and that LAIR-2 releases LAIR-1-mediated immune suppression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their understanding of the system.

claim: Collagens, LAIR-1 and LAIR-2 have unique and overlapping associations with survival in certain tumors.
source: Analysis of public human datasets shows that collagens, LAIR-1 and LAIR-2 have unique and overlapping associations with survival in certain tumors.
evidence: This is supported by the TCGA analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: NC410 is a dimeric LAIR-2 with a functional IgG1 Fc tail.
source: We designed a dimeric LAIR-2 with a functional IgG1 Fc tail, NC410, and showed that NC410 increases human T cell expansion and effector function in vivo in a mouse xenogeneic-graft versus-host disease model.
evidence: This is a description of the therapeutic molecule designed by the authors.

claim: NC410 increases human T cell expansion and effector function in vivo in a mouse xenogeneic-graft versus-host disease model.
source: We designed a dimeric LAIR-2 with a functional IgG1 Fc tail, NC410, and showed that NC410 increases human T cell expansion and effector function in vivo in a mouse xenogeneic-graft versus-host disease model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: In humanized mouse tumor models, NC410 reduces tumor growth that is dependent on T cells.
source: In humanized mouse tumor models, NC410 reduces tumor growth that is dependent on T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: NC410 binds to collagen-rich areas where LAIR-1+ immune cells are localized in human tumors.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis of human tumors shows that NC410 binds to collagen-rich areas where LAIR-1+ immune cells are localized.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data presented in Figure 7.

claim: NC410 might be a novel strategy for cancer immunotherapy for immune-excluded tumors.
source: Our findings show that NC410 might be a novel strategy for cancer immunotherapy for immune-excluded tumors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Not all patients show the same degree of response to immune checkpoint blockade therapies.
source: However, not all patients show the same degree of response and not all tumors respond to these therapies (Gibney et al., 2016; Darvin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Not all tumors respond to immune checkpoint blockade therapies.
source: However, not all patients show the same degree of response and not all tumors respond to these therapies (Gibney et al., 2016; Darvin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: At least 28 different collagens comprising at least 43 genes have been identified.
source: At least 28 different collagens comprising at least 43 genes have been identified (Myllyharju and Kivirikko, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The ECM functions as a scaffold for tissue organization.
source: The ECM functions not only as a scaffold for tissue organization but also provides critical biochemical and biomechanical cues that instruct cell growth, survival, differentiation and migration and regulate vascular development and immune function (Hynes, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The ECM provides critical biochemical and biomechanical cues that instruct cell growth, survival, differentiation and migration.
source: The ECM functions not only as a scaffold for tissue organization but also provides critical biochemical and biomechanical cues that instruct cell growth, survival, differentiation and migration and regulate vascular development and immune function (Hynes, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The ECM regulates vascular development and immune function.
source: The ECM functions not only as a scaffold for tissue organization but also provides critical biochemical and biomechanical cues that instruct cell growth, survival, differentiation and migration and regulate vascular development and immune function (Hynes, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Several epithelial tumors including breast, pancreatic, colorectal, ovarian and lung cancer are characterized by a dense ECM where high collagen content correlates with poor prognosis.
source: Several epithelial tumors including breast, pancreatic, colorectal, ovarian and lung cancer are characterized by a dense ECM where high collagen content correlates with poor prognosis (Fang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: ECM or 'Matrisome' signatures associated with tumor type and stage of disease have been described.
source: Indeed, ECM or 'Matrisome' signatures associated with tumor type and stage of disease have been described (Levental et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2012; Naba et al., 2012; Naba et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts, macrophages and tumor cells themselves all contribute to increased collagen production and remodeling during cancer progression.
source: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) (Kalluri, 2016), macrophages and tumor cells themselves (Naba et al., 2012; Januchowski et al., 2014; Naba et al., 2014a) all contribute to increased collagen production and remodeling during cancer progression.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most tumors overexpress a diverse set of collagens in an abnormal fashion.
source: Most tumors overexpress a diverse set of collagens in an abnormal fashion (Nissen et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Overexpression of collagens has been associated with poor overall survival in several tumor types, such as lung, colorectal and ovarian cancer.
source: Overexpression of collagens has been associated with poor overall survival in several tumor types, such as lung (Iizasa et al., 2004; Ke et al., 2014), colorectal (Naba et al., 2014b; Huang et al., 2018) and ovarian cancer (Cheon et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Abnormal collagen production, composition and organization in the TME is a cause of immune dysfunction, conveying a chronic-active wound-healing response instead of anti-tumor immune responses.
source: We now consider abnormal collagen production, composition and organization in the TME as a cause of immune dysfunction, conveying a chronic-active wound-healing response instead of anti-tumor immune responses necessary for immune surveillance and the eradication of the tumor (Antonio et al., 2015; Rosowski and Huttenlocher, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The abnormal ECM builds physical fibrotic barriers to exclude immune cells and therapeutic agents from access to tumor cells.
source: The abnormal ECM also builds physical fibrotic barriers to exclude immune cells and therapeutic agents from access to tumor cells (Henke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TME-expressed collagen can interact directly with the inhibitory collagen receptor LAIR-1.
source: TME-expressed collagen can interact directly with the inhibitory collagen receptor leukocyte-associated immunoglobulin-like receptor 1 (LAIR-1) (Rygiel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: LAIR-1 is an immune checkpoint broadly expressed on the cell surface of immune cells.
source: LAIR-1 is an immune checkpoint broadly expressed on the cell surface of immune cells (Meyaard et al., 1997) that binds to collagen (Lebbink et al., 2006) and molecules with collagen-like domains (Son et al., 2012; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LAIR-1 binds to collagen.
source: LAIR-1 is an immune checkpoint broadly expressed on the cell surface of immune cells (Meyaard et al., 1997) that binds to collagen (Lebbink et al., 2006) and molecules with collagen-like domains (Son et al., 2012; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LAIR-1 binds to molecules with collagen-like domains.
source: LAIR-1 is an immune checkpoint broadly expressed on the cell surface of immune cells (Meyaard et al., 1997) that binds to collagen (Lebbink et al., 2006) and molecules with collagen-like domains (Son et al., 2012; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LAIR-1+ cells strongly adhere to collagen.
source: LAIR-1+ cells strongly adhere to collagen (Lebbink et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits NK cell function.
source: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits NK cell (Meyaard et al., 1997), T cell (Maasho et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2014; Park et al., 2020), B cell (van der Vuurst de Vries et al., 1999; Merlo et al., 2005), monocyte (Son and Diamond, 2015) and DC function (Poggi et al., 1998; Son et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits T cell function.
source: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits NK cell (Meyaard et al., 1997), T cell (Maasho et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2014; Park et al., 2020), B cell (van der Vuurst de Vries et al., 1999; Merlo et al., 2005), monocyte (Son and Diamond, 2015) and DC function (Poggi et al., 1998; Son et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits B cell function.
source: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits NK cell (Meyaard et al., 1997), T cell (Maasho et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2014; Park et al., 2020), B cell (van der Vuurst de Vries et al., 1999; Merlo et al., 2005), monocyte (Son and Diamond, 2015) and DC function (Poggi et al., 1998; Son et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits monocyte function.
source: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits NK cell (Meyaard et al., 1997), T cell (Maasho et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2014; Park et al., 2020), B cell (van der Vuurst de Vries et al., 1999; Merlo et al., 2005), monocyte (Son and Diamond, 2015) and DC function (Poggi et al., 1998; Son et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits DC function.
source: Upon triggering, LAIR-1 inhibits NK cell (Meyaard et al., 1997), T cell (Maasho et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2014; Park et al., 2020), B cell (van der Vuurst de Vries et al., 1999; Merlo et al., 2005), monocyte (Son and Diamond, 2015) and DC function (Poggi et al., 1998; Son et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TME-expressed collagens can function to promote immune evasion through their direct interaction with LAIR-1.
source: Thus, besides formation of an ECM-rich and fibrotic tumor niche, TME-expressed collagens can function to promote immune evasion through their direct interaction with LAIR-1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature and the authors' understanding of the system.

claim: LAIR-2 is a natural soluble homolog of LAIR-1 that is present in humans and non-human primates, but not other animals.
source: LAIR-2 is a natural soluble homolog of LAIR-1 that is present in humans and non-human primates, but not other animals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LAIR-2.

claim: LAIR-2 shares 83% identity with the LAIR-1 extracellular region.
source: LAIR-2 shares 83% identity with the LAIR-1 extracellular region, binds to collagens with higher affinity than LAIR-1 and functions as a natural antagonist to block cell membrane LAIR-1 inhibitory signaling (Lebbink, Lebbink et al., 2008; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LAIR-2 binds to collagens with higher affinity than LAIR-1.
source: LAIR-2 shares 83% identity with the LAIR-1 extracellular region, binds to collagens with higher affinity than LAIR-1 and functions as a natural antagonist to block cell membrane LAIR-1 inhibitory signaling (Lebbink, Lebbink et al., 2008; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LAIR-2 functions as a natural antagonist to block cell membrane LAIR-1 inhibitory signaling.
source: LAIR-2 shares 83% identity with the LAIR-1 extracellular region, binds to collagens with higher affinity than LAIR-1 and functions as a natural antagonist to block cell membrane LAIR-1 inhibitory signaling (Lebbink, Lebbink et al., 2008; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: 10 out of 21 tumors had reduced overall survival with high overall levels of collagens.
source: When we examined the mRNA expression of all 43 collagen genes combined, 10 out of 21 tumors had reduced overall survival with high (quantile) overall levels of collagens (Figure 1A, Source code 1).
evidence: This is supported by the TCGA analysis presented in Figure 1A.

claim: LAIR-1 expression was significantly upregulated in 11 of 21 tumors when evaluated by TCGA data.
source: Likewise, the LAIR-1 expression was significantly upregulated in 11 of 21 tumors when evaluated by TCGA data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Source code 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by the TCGA analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LAIR-1 expression is observed in all tumor types and largely restricted to immune cells.
source: LAIR-1 expression is observed in all tumor types and largely restricted to immune cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the TCGA data analysis.

claim: Patients with high LAIR-1 mRNA expression had lower survival probability in four tumor types.
source: By stratifying patients for high- and low-quantile LAIR-1 mRNA expression, we observed that patients with high LAIR-1 mRNA expression had lower survival probability in four tumor types (Figure 1B, Source code 4).
evidence: This is supported by the TCGA analysis presented in Figure 1B.

claim: A unique set of tumor types emerged when patients were stratified for high or low expression of all collagens combined with high or low LAIR-1 for overall survival analysis.
source: We further stratified the patients in the TCGA database to include high or low expression of all collagens combined with high or low LAIR-1 for overall survival analysis (Figure 1C, Source code 5). A unique set of tumor types emerged that overlapped with those with significant increased LAIR-1 expression, but only partially with the tumor types in that of the total collagen overall survival analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the TCGA analysis presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Six tumor types had improved overall survival with high expression of LAIR-2.
source: TCGA evaluation demonstrated that six tumor types had improved overall survival with high (quantile) expression of LAIR-2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the TCGA analysis presented in Figure 2A.

claim: LAIR-2 expression levels are relatively low in most tumors in comparison to LAIR-1.
source: This was despite relatively low expression levels of LAIR-2 in most tumors in comparison to LAIR-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Source code 3).
evidence: This is supported by the TCGA analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NC410 bound to human collagen I and III with high avidity.
source: NC410 bound to human collagen I and III with high avidity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the Octet analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: NC410 is cross-reactive to rat and mouse collagens.
source: While LAIR-2 is not present in rodents, it is cross-reactive to rat and mouse collagens due to the highly conserved nature of collagens across species (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the Octet analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: NC410 completely blocked human LAIR-1 binding to collagen I.
source: NC410 completely blocked human LAIR-1 binding to collagen I since LAIR-2 binds with higher affinity to collagens than human LAIR-1, as reported previously (Lebbink et al., 2008; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2011), supporting its potential role as a LAIR-1 antagonist therapeutic (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the binding assay presented in Figure 2D.

claim: NC410 inhibited collagen-mediated LAIR-1 signaling in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: Using flow cytometry (Figure 2E) and Incucyte microscope imaging (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we observed a dose-dependent inhibition of LAIR-1 NFAT-GFP reporter activity by NC410, indicating that NC410 inhibited collagen-mediated LAIR-1 signaling in a dose-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is supported by the reporter assay data presented in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: The majority of human T cells in the spleen on day 6 post transfer acquired an effector memory phenotype as a percentage of total T cells irrespective of treatment.
source: Figure 3A, B shows that the majority of human T cells in the spleen on day 6 post transfer acquired an effector memory (EM, CD45RA-CCR7-) phenotype as a percentage of total T cells irrespective of treatment (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for gating strategy).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: With increasing doses of NC410, there was a trend of effector T cell expansion as a percentage of total T cells.
source: However, it was noted that with increasing doses of NC410, there was a trend of effector T cell (CD45RA+CCR7-) expansion as a percentage of total T cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: NC410 significantly increased the number of human CD4+EM T cells in the spleen in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: In the spleen, it was found that NC410 significantly increased the number of human CD4+EM T cells and human CD8+ effector T cells in a dose-dependent fashion (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: NC410 significantly increased the number of human CD8+ effector T cells in the spleen in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: In the spleen, it was found that NC410 significantly increased the number of human CD4+EM T cells and human CD8+ effector T cells in a dose-dependent fashion (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: NC410 treatment at 1 mg/kg resulted in significantly reduced tumor growth of P815.
source: Treatment resulted in significantly reduced tumor growth of P815 in the 1 mg/kg treatment group, but not the 3 and 10 mg/kg treatment groups (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor growth data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: NC410 promoted the expansion of both human CD8+ and CD4+ T cells on days 6 and 13.
source: NC410 promoted the expansion of both human CD8+ and CD4+ T cells on days 6 and 13.
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figures 4D-G.

claim: NC410 at 10 mg/kg resulted in a greater increase in T cell numbers on day 6.
source: Interestingly, the kinetics of T cell expansion and/or retention changed with dose level. NC410 at 10 mg/kg resulted in a greater increase in T cell numbers on day 6 (Figure 4D, F), while 1 mg/kg resulted in the highest T cell numbers on day 13 (Figure 4E, G).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: NC410 at 1 mg/kg resulted in the highest T cell numbers on day 13.
source: Interestingly, the kinetics of T cell expansion and/or retention changed with dose level. NC410 at 10 mg/kg resulted in a greater increase in T cell numbers on day 6 (Figure 4D, F), while 1 mg/kg resulted in the highest T cell numbers on day 13 (Figure 4E, G).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: The sustained expansion of human T cells with a lower dose of NC410 correlated with control of tumor growth.
source: Together, these results suggested that the sustained expansion of human T cells with a lower dose of NC410 correlated with control of tumor growth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: NC410 treatment at 10 mg/kg significantly reduced tumor growth compared to isotype control in the HT-29 model.
source: NC410 treatment at 10 mg/kg significantly reduced tumor growth compared to isotype control (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor growth data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: NC410 at 10 mg/kg appeared optimal in the HT-29 model.
source: In a follow-up dose-titration experiment, it was found that NC410 at 10 mg/kg appeared optimal in the HT-29 model (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor growth data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: HT-29 cells express collagens.
source: Because HT-29 cells also express collagens (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3), we investigated whether binding of NC410 to HT-29 cells elicits ADCC.
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression and immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: No differences in HT-29 killing by PBMC were observed between NC410, isotype and medium-treated samples in an in vitro chromium release cytotoxicity assay.
source: In an in vitro chromium release cytotoxicity assay, no differences in HT-29 killing by PBMC were observed between NC410, isotype and medium-treated samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F), suggesting that the anti-tumor effect of NC410 is not mediated by ADCC.
evidence: This is supported by the cytotoxicity assay data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F.

claim: The anti-tumor effect of NC410 is not mediated by ADCC.
source: In an in vitro chromium release cytotoxicity assay, no differences in HT-29 killing by PBMC were observed between NC410, isotype and medium-treated samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F), suggesting that the anti-tumor effect of NC410 is not mediated by ADCC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cytotoxicity assay data.

claim: The therapeutic effect of NC410 was abrogated when T cell-depleted PBMC were transferred into NSG mice.
source: In agreement, the therapeutic effect of NC410 was abrogated when we transferred T cell-depleted PBMC into NSG mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor growth data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: T cells are required for the anti-tumor effect mediated by NC410.
source: Thus, T cells are required for the anti-tumor effect mediated by NC410, arguing against ADCC as the main effector mechanism in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the T cell depletion experiment.

claim: Both T cells and a functional Fc were required for NC410 anti-tumor activity and decreased tumor growth.
source: Thus, both T cells and a functional Fc were required for NC410 anti-tumor activity and decreased tumor growth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the T cell depletion and LAIR-2-FES experiments.

claim: There was a significant increase in the number of human CD4+ T cells in tumors treated with NC410 compared to control.
source: Analysis of T cell numbers within the tumor showed a significant increase in the number of human CD4+ and a trend towards increased CD8+ T cell numbers in tumors treated with NC410 compared to control (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: There was a trend towards increased CD8+ T cell numbers in tumors treated with NC410 compared to control.
source: Analysis of T cell numbers within the tumor showed a significant increase in the number of human CD4+ and a trend towards increased CD8+ T cell numbers in tumors treated with NC410 compared to control (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: A significant increase in IFN-γ+ and IFN-γ+TNF-α+ double-positive cells was observed in the NC410 treatment group compared to control after re-stimulation.
source: After re-stimulation, a significant increase in IFN-γ+ and IFN-γ+TNF-α+ double-positive cells was observed in the NC410 treatment group compared to control.
evidence: This is supported by the intracellular cytokine staining data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: IFN-γ and granzyme B were significantly increased in the TME.
source: Analysis of cytokines indicated that IFN-γ and granzyme B were significantly increased in the TME, but not soluble CD40L (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by the Luminex data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Increased expression of CD40L and granzyme B was observed in the spleen.
source: Increased expression of CD40L and granzyme B was observed in the spleen (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by the Luminex data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: CXCL10, CXCL11 and CXCL12 were all significantly increased in the TME.
source: Chemokine analysis indicated that CXCL10, CXCL11 and CXCL12 were all significantly increased in the TME (Figure 5H), and significantly decreased in the spleen (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by the Luminex data presented in Figure 5H.

claim: CXCL10, CXCL11 and CXCL12 were significantly decreased in the spleen.
source: Chemokine analysis indicated that CXCL10, CXCL11 and CXCL12 were all significantly increased in the TME (Figure 5H), and significantly decreased in the spleen (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by the Luminex data presented in Figure 5I.

claim: The concentration of CXCL10, CXCL11 and CXCL12 correlated with tumor reduction.
source: Importantly, the concentration of all three chemokines correlated with tumor reduction (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 5J.

claim: NC410 has the capacity to induce T cell expansion, T cell tumor infiltration and reduction of tumor growth in vivo.
source: Thus, we established that NC410 has the capacity to induce T cell expansion, T cell tumor infiltration and reduction of tumor growth in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in Figures 3-5.

claim: C6M and C4G were significantly increased at week 4 in the NC410-treated group in comparison to the control group.
source: Two of the CDPs, namely C6M (a collagen VI MMP-2 CDP) and C4G (a collagen IV granzyme B CDP), were significantly increased at week 4 in the NC410-treated group in comparison to the control group (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the CDP analysis presented in Figure 6C.

claim: The increase in serum CDPs was observed at the time of NC410-mediated tumor eradication, suggesting that the CDPs were derived from the tumor as a result of T cell activation and effector function.
source: Interestingly, this increase in serum CDPs was observed at the time of NC410-mediated tumor eradication, suggesting that the CDPs were derived from the tumor as a result of T cell activation and effector function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal correlation between CDP increase and tumor eradication.

claim: NC410 binding co-localized with Masson's Trichrome-positive collagen areas within the TME.
source: NC410 binding co-localized with Masson's Trichrome-positive collagen areas within the TME and LAIR-1+ immune cells was present in all tumors (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, healthy tissue Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: LAIR-1+ immune cells were present in all tumors.
source: NC410 binding co-localized with Masson's Trichrome-positive collagen areas within the TME and LAIR-1+ immune cells was present in all tumors (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, healthy tissue Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both myeloid and lymphoid cells within the TME expressed LAIR-1.
source: Both myeloid and lymphoid cells within the TME expressed LAIR-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: NC410 binding was highest in PDAC in agreement with a collagen-rich TME.
source: NC410 binding was highest in PDAC in agreement with a collagen-rich TME (Figure 7C), and HNSC had the highest number of LAIR-1+ cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry quantification presented in Figure 7C.

claim: HNSC had the highest number of LAIR-1+ cells.
source: NC410 binding was highest in PDAC in agreement with a collagen-rich TME (Figure 7C), and HNSC had the highest number of LAIR-1+ cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry quantification presented in Figure 7D.

claim: LAIR-1+ cells were enriched in NC410-positive areas.
source: Importantly, LAIR-1+ cells were enriched in NC410-positive areas (Figure 7E), suggesting that LAIR-1+ cells were entrapped in the collagen matrix.
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: LAIR-1+ cells were entrapped in the collagen matrix.
source: Importantly, LAIR-1+ cells were enriched in NC410-positive areas (Figure 7E), suggesting that LAIR-1+ cells were entrapped in the collagen matrix.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-localization of LAIR-1+ cells and NC410 binding.

claim: NC410 binding was particularly increased in immune-excluded tumors.
source: By characterizing our cohort according to these immunological phenotypes, we observed that NC410 binding was particularly increased in immune-excluded tumors (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry quantification presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: In immune-excluded tumors, LAIR-1+ cells may be sequestered in collagen-rich areas where NC410 can bind and disrupt LAIR-1-mediated inhibition and adhesion.
source: Thus, in immune-excluded tumors, LAIR-1+ cells may be sequestered in collagen-rich areas where NC410 can bind and disrupt LAIR-1-mediated inhibition and adhesion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the immunohistochemistry data showing NC410 binding in immune-excluded tumors.

claim: Tumor progression is accompanied by extensive remodeling of the ECM, leading to the formation of a tumor-specific ECM, which is often more collagen-rich and of increased stiffness.
source: Tumor progression is accompanied by extensive remodeling of the ECM, leading to the formation of a tumor-specific ECM, which is often more collagen-rich and of increased stiffness (Cox and Erler, 2014; Pickup et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Collagen expression and density have been shown to be associated with a worse prognosis either by directly promoting tumor growth or by preventing immune cell infiltration.
source: Collagen expression and density have been shown to be associated with a worse prognosis either by directly promoting tumor growth or by preventing immune cell infiltration (Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Collagens can directly modulate T cell function.
source: It has been demonstrated that collagens can directly modulate T cell function (Salmon et al., 2012; Hartmann et al., 2014; Kuczek et al., 2019), for instance, through the inhibitory collagen receptor LAIR-1 (Rygiel et al., 2011; Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: High expression of total collagens, LAIR-1, and combined high total collagen and high LAIR-1 are associated with a worse prognosis in multiple tumor types.
source: We showed by RNA analysis that high expression of total collagens, LAIR-1, and combined high total collagen and high LAIR-1 are associated with a worse prognosis in multiple tumor types, supporting the notion of disrupting LAIR-1-collagen interactions as a novel immunotherapeutic strategy.
evidence: This is supported by the TCGA analysis presented in Figure 1.

claim: LAIR-2 can be found in vivo in the urine from pregnant women and in fluids such as synovial fluid of rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis patients and the circulation of patients with autoimmune thyroid disease.
source: LAIR-2 can be found in vivo in the urine from pregnant women and in fluids such as synovial fluid of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and osteoarthritis (OA) patients and the circulation of patients with autoimmune thyroid disease ( Lebbink et al., 2008; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2011; Simone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The amount of LAIR-2 protein seems to be related to inflammation.
source: The amount of LAIR-2 protein seems to be related to inflammation (Olde Nordkamp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In vitro stimulation of sorted peripheral blood cells revealed that CD4+ T cells are the main producers of LAIR-2.
source: In vitro stimulation of sorted peripheral blood cells revealed that CD4+ T cells are the main producers of LAIR-2 (Olde Nordkamp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Targeting and disrupting collagen interactions with LAIR-1 by means of NC410 promoted in vivo T cell activity and had a therapeutic effect in tumor models, which was dependent on T cells.
source: In this study, we showed that targeting and disrupting collagen interactions with LAIR-1 by means of a dimeric LAIR-2 hIgG1 Fc fusion protein, NC410, promoted in vivo T cell activity and had a therapeutic effect in tumor models, which was dependent on T cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Peak activity of NC410 was observed at different doses in the P815 (1 mg/kg) vs. HT-29 (10 mg/kg) tumor model.
source: It is interesting to note that we observed peak activity of NC410 at different doses in the P815 (1 mg/kg) vs. HT-29 (10 mg/kg) tumor model.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: LAIR-2 IgG1 protein with a 'silenced' Fc (FES mutation) loses anti-tumor activity.
source: However, to further address the question of what the Fc portion of NC410 does, we show that LAIR-2 IgG1 protein with a 'silenced' Fc (FES mutation) (Oganesyan et al., 2008) loses anti-tumor activity.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: A recent independently published study demonstrates anti-tumor activity with an engineered LAIR-2 Fc protein.
source: A recent independently published study (Xu et al., 2020) also demonstrates anti-tumor activity with an engineered LAIR-2 Fc protein.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: NC410 may have additional LAIR-1-independent mechanisms of action since LAIR-2 Fc can efficiently inhibit complement activation via classical and lectin pathways.
source: NC410 may also have additional LAIR-1-independent mechanisms of action since we have previously shown that LAIR-2 Fc can efficiently inhibit complement activation via classical and lectin pathways (Olde Nordkamp et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is a speculation based on previously published work.

claim: A limitation of the humanized model with adoptive transfer of PBMCs is the absence of human myeloid cells.
source: While our study demonstrated that the anti-tumor effect promoted by NC410 required T cells, a limitation of the humanized model with adoptive transfer of PBMCs is the absence of human myeloid cells (Ali et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a known limitation of the experimental model, supported by a citation.

claim: Serum levels of collagen degradation fragments are elevated in cancer patients compared to healthy controls.
source: Serum levels of collagen degradation fragments are elevated in cancer patients compared to healthy controls, and checkpoint blockade alters serum CDP levels (Jensen et al., 2018; Jensen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Checkpoint blockade alters serum CDP levels.
source: Serum levels of collagen degradation fragments are elevated in cancer patients compared to healthy controls, and checkpoint blockade alters serum CDP levels (Jensen et al., 2018; Jensen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Granzyme B promotes cytotoxic lymphocyte transmigration via basement membrane remodeling of type IV collagen.
source: Indeed, granzyme B promotes cytotoxic lymphocyte transmigration via basement membrane remodeling of type IV collagen (Prakash et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Granzyme B-degraded type IV collagen fragments (C4G) associate with favorable anti-CTLA-4 treatment response in metastatic melanoma patients.
source: Interestingly, granzyme B-degraded type IV collagen fragments (C4G) associate with favorable anti-CTLA-4 treatment response in metastatic melanoma patients (Jensen et al., 2018; Jensen et al., 2020; St-Pierre and Potworowski, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NC410 showed decreased tumor growth as a monotherapy.
source: NC410 showed decreased tumor growth as a monotherapy, but it might even show better clinical efficacy when used in combination with currently used checkpoint receptor inhibitors such as CTLA4 and/or PD-1.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NC410 might show better clinical efficacy when used in combination with currently used checkpoint receptor inhibitors such as CTLA4 and/or PD-1.
source: NC410 showed decreased tumor growth as a monotherapy, but it might even show better clinical efficacy when used in combination with currently used checkpoint receptor inhibitors such as CTLA4 and/or PD-1.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential future applications.

claim: Abrogating LAIR-1 immunosuppression through LAIR-2 overexpression or SHP-1 inhibition sensitizes resistant lung tumors to anti-PD-1 therapy.
source: In accordance, it was recently shown that abrogating LAIR-1 immunosuppression through LAIR-2 overexpression or SHP-1 inhibition sensitizes resistant lung tumors to anti-PD-1 therapy (Peng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Circulating LAIR-2 protein concentration is low or undetectable in healthy individuals.
source: Circulating LAIR-2 protein concentration is low or undetectable in healthy individuals (Lebbink et al., 2008; Olde Nordkamp et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the presence of limited endogenous LAIR-2, LAIR-1 can bind collagens, thereby allowing the inhibitory receptor to signal and prevent or reduce T cell activity and/or retain LAIR-1+ cells in collagen-rich areas.
source: In the presence of limited endogenous LAIR-2, LAIR-1 can bind collagens, thereby allowing the inhibitory receptor to signal and prevent or reduce T cell activity and/or retain LAIR-1+ cells in collagen-rich areas.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known biology of LAIR-1 and LAIR-2.

claim: In the TME, increased levels of collagens will promote tumor immune escape in the absence of increased LAIR-2.
source: In the TME, increased levels of collagens will therefore promote tumor immune escape in the absence of increased LAIR-2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known biology of LAIR-1 and LAIR-2.

claim: Enhanced expression of endogenous LAIR-2 in some tumors associated with better prognosis.
source: Our analysis of TCGA data indeed revealed that enhanced expression of endogenous LAIR-2 in some tumors associated with better prognosis, suggesting that further increasing LAIR-2 in vivo could have a therapeutic advantage.
evidence: This is supported by the TCGA analysis presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Further increasing LAIR-2 in vivo could have a therapeutic advantage.
source: Our analysis of TCGA data indeed revealed that enhanced expression of endogenous LAIR-2 in some tumors associated with better prognosis, suggesting that further increasing LAIR-2 in vivo could have a therapeutic advantage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TCGA analysis.

claim: NC410 has a higher avidity to collagen than endogenous LAIR-2 due to its dimeric structure.
source: NC410 has a higher avidity to collagen than endogenous LAIR-2 due to its dimeric structure since in vivo LAIR-2 is expressed as a monomer, enhancing its potential to block the inhibitory capacity of membrane-bound LAIR-1.
evidence: This is based on the known structural properties of NC410 and endogenous LAIR-2.

claim: In vivo LAIR-2 is expressed as a monomer.
source: NC410 has a higher avidity to collagen than endogenous LAIR-2 due to its dimeric structure since in vivo LAIR-2 is expressed as a monomer, enhancing its potential to block the inhibitory capacity of membrane-bound LAIR-1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LAIR-2.

claim: NC410 binds both healthy and tumoral collagen.
source: NC410 binds both healthy and tumoral collagen and theoretically could be sequestered before reaching the tumor site.
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The avidity of NC410 towards tumoral collagen is higher than to healthy collagen.
source: We hypothesize that the avidity of NC410 towards tumoral collagen is higher than to healthy collagen, therefore resulting in a therapeutic effect, but this needs additional study.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: C1q has been shown to be increased in tumors.
source: Other LAIR-1 ligands, such as C1q, have been shown to be increased in tumors (Bulla et al., 2016) and may also provide a local inhibitory effect that could be potentially reversed by NC410.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: C1q may provide a local inhibitory effect that could be potentially reversed by NC410.
source: Other LAIR-1 ligands, such as C1q, have been shown to be increased in tumors (Bulla et al., 2016) and may also provide a local inhibitory effect that could be potentially reversed by NC410.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms of action.

claim: The immune-excluded phenotype is characterized by the presence of immune cells that cannot penetrate the parenchyma of the tumors but instead are located in the stroma that surrounds the tumor cells.
source: The immune-excluded phenotype is characterized by the presence of immune cells that cannot penetrate the parenchyma of the tumors but instead are located in the stroma that surrounds the tumor cells (Chen and Mellman, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Immune-excluded tumors currently fare poorly with PD-1/PD-L1 immunotherapy.
source: These are indications that currently fare poorly with PD-1/PD-L1 immunotherapy (Jiang et al., 2018), and thus NC410 could benefit an entirely new class of cancer patients when used as either a monotherapy or in combination with checkpoint inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: NC410 could benefit an entirely new class of cancer patients when used as either a monotherapy or in combination with checkpoint inhibitors.
source: These are indications that currently fare poorly with PD-1/PD-L1 immunotherapy (Jiang et al., 2018), and thus NC410 could benefit an entirely new class of cancer patients when used as either a monotherapy or in combination with checkpoint inhibitors.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications.

claim: NC410 is a novel immunomedicine for targeting immune-excluded collagen-rich tumors and enabling normalization of the tumor-immune microenvironment.
source: Our data support NC410 as a novel immunomedicine for targeting immune-excluded collagen-rich tumors and enabling normalization of the tumor-immune microenvironment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A first-in-human phase I clinical trial is currently ongoing to test the safety and tolerability of NC410.
source: A first-in-human phase I clinical trial is currently ongoing to test the safety and tolerability of NC410.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about an ongoing clinical trial.

claim: The potential of C6M and C4G collagen fragments as biomarkers of clinical response will be further investigated in a recently initiated NC410 first-in-human clinical trial (NCT04408599).
source: The potential of C6M and C4G collagen fragments as biomarkers of clinical response will be further investigated in a recently initiated NC410 first-in-human clinical trial (NCT04408599).
evidence: This is a statement about future research plans.
